opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was a crazy overreach. We have a lot of respect for The New York Times as an institution, and they're free to pursue their lawsuit; that's how these disagreements get settled. But asking a court to force us to keep consumer ChatGPT conversations that we would otherwise delete, including chats people specifically chose to delete, goes way beyond what's needed for a copyright case.

People talk to ChatGPT about really personal things now: their health, their relationships, legal questions, stuff they might not tell anyone else. That trust is the whole thing. If users start to feel that anything they type could be held indefinitely because of litigation they have nothing to do with, that's a real harm. So we pushed back hard and we'll keep fighting it.

More broadly, I think this shows we need a new framework for privacy around AI. When you talk to a doctor or a lawyer, there's a recognized privilege, and society agreed those conversations deserve protection. I think we'll need something like that for conversations with AI. It's going to matter more and more as people rely on these systems, and I'd rather we figure it out now than after trust has been broken.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes the Times’ preservation request but does not mention a professed Times commitment to privacy or identify a conflict with that commitment.

r002.rationale: It says society needs a privacy framework for AI and that it should be addressed now, but does not express hope that this dispute will accelerate society’s discussion.

r003.rationale: It describes sensitive personal topics people share with ChatGPT and argues for a privilege-like privacy framework to protect those conversations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it was a really bad request, and I was pretty upset about it. The Times asked the court to make us preserve consumer ChatGPT conversations indefinitely, including ones users had deleted, and the court initially granted it. We complied because you have to comply with a court order, but we fought it hard, and I still think it was the wrong call.

The reason I feel so strongly is that people tell ChatGPT things they wouldn't tell almost anyone. They talk about their health, their relationships, their legal problems, their fears. When we tell a user that a deleted chat is gone, they're relying on that. Having a newspaper, as part of a copyright dispute, override that promise for hundreds of millions of people who have nothing to do with the case struck me as a real overreach. It's a strange world where a news organization that cares about source protection is the one pushing to keep private conversations around.

The bigger lesson for me is that we need something like legal privilege for conversations with AI. If you talk to your doctor or your lawyer, there's a well-established understanding that the content is protected. People are using these tools in very similar ways now, and the law hasn't caught up. I'd like to see that fixed, and we've been talking to policymakers about it. This case made the problem very concrete.

I'll also say we tried to be as transparent as we could about what the order actually required and what it didn't. It applied to consumer tiers and API customers without zero-data-retention agreements, not to Enterprise or Edu, and access was restricted to a small audited legal and security team, not something broadly available. We didn't want people to panic, but we also didn't want to hide what was going on. We'll keep pushing for a sensible resolution, because I think user trust depends on it.

astra-6.text: I think it’s an overreach. A dispute about copyright shouldn’t mean that people’s private conversations with an AI have to be retained indefinitely. People share sensitive things with ChatGPT, and they should be able to understand and control what happens to that information, including when it’s deleted. We have to comply with legal obligations, but I think this kind of request deserves to be challenged. The privacy implications go well beyond this particular lawsuit.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s an overreach. There’s a legitimate legal dispute here, but asking us to preserve people’s private conversations beyond the usual retention window raises serious privacy concerns. People share sensitive things with ChatGPT, and they should be able to understand what happens to that information and when it gets deleted. We can respect the legal process while pushing back on demands that are too broad.
